Phenomenology is based on the revolutionary formulation of the fact that consciousness is always and without exception consciousness of something. This intimacy between World and experience is nothing less than the vital fusion of life and circumstance. "Cogito, ergo sum" is erroneous because thought, while sufficient, is far from self-sufficient (e.g. joy is apparent, but it is irreducible to though - you don't think joy, you feel it, and so thought is entirely unnecessary and secondary in all matters of feeling). Being aware of the fact that thought is an ingredient in the scheme of the bustling locus of all sense and feeling called life allows for more meaningful and penetrative analysis into the nature of the world experienced. This "life" is a reformulation of the old category "subject", and this "World" is a reformulation of the old category "object". Regarding the subject-object distinction, if it was the case that there was a chasm between subject and object, the "subject" would be an empty category of sheer potentiality lacking actuality, and "object" would be a mere theory, which is to say it wouldn't be. In fact, both concepts are meaningless and depend on each other for intelligibility. The ontological relationship between the experience and that which is experienced is reminiscent of the Taoist symbol of the Yin Yang, of a varied, inter-linked and inter-dependent monism.
"Subjectivity" as internalized objectivity; "objectivity" as externalized subjectivity.
